19188: What does the Bible mean by the 'restoration of all things', and does it mean that everyone will finally be saved?
19189: In Acts 3:21 Peter says Jesus must stay in heaven 'until the times of restoration of all things' that God spoke about through the prophets. The Greek word for restoration, *apokatastasis*, became famous because some early theologians, especially Origen and Gregory of Nyssa, used it for the hope that every person (and perhaps even the devil) would finally be reconciled to God. But the word itself is broad. In context it can mean the restoration of Israel and God's kingdom, or the renewal of the whole creation, without saying anything about every individual. Christians have read the related verses in all three ways, and the universalist reading has strong modern defenders and strong traditional objections. Whether the church formally condemned universalism in 543 and 553 is itself debated by historians.
19190: *Apokatastasis* simply means 'restoration'; the word alone does not settle who or what is restored.
19191: In Acts, the nearest context is the restoration of Israel and the kingdom (Acts 1:6, Acts 3:19-21).
19192: Texts like Colossians 1:20, Ephesians 1:10 and 1 Corinthians 15:28 speak of God reconciling or uniting 'all things', which many read as cosmic renewal.
19193: Origen, Gregory of Nyssa and Isaac the Syrian hoped for the restoration of all persons; modern defenders include David Bentley Hart, Thomas Talbott and Robin Parry.
19194: Traditional objections point to texts about final, eternal judgment and to the role of human freedom.
19195: Justinian's edict of 543 and the anathemas linked to the council of 553 condemned an Origenist system, but whether they bind the church against every form of universal hope is disputed.
19197:
The Greek noun *apokatastasis* and its verb *apokathistēmi* mean 'to restore' or 'put back into a former state'. In ordinary Greek they were used for healing a limb, returning property, or the planets returning to an earlier position.

The Gospels use the verb for healing: a withered hand is 'restored' (Mark 3:5). The Greek Old Testament uses it in Malachi's promise that Elijah will 'restore' the hearts of fathers to their children (Mal 4:5-6), which Jesus echoes when he says Elijah comes and 'will restore all things' (Matt 17:11). The disciples ask the risen Jesus whether he will now 'restore the kingdom to Israel' (Acts 1:6).

So the word is about restoration in general. What is being restored, and to what, has to be learned from the context each time.
19198: Myth: 'The word apokatastasis in Acts 3:21 proves universal salvation.' Correction: the word simply means restoration. Universalists build their case on several texts and theological arguments, not on this word alone, and most universalist scholars admit Acts 3:21 is not decisive by itself.
19200:
Peter is speaking to a Jewish crowd in the temple after healing a lame man. He calls them to repent 'that times of refreshing may come', so that God may send the Messiah, 'whom heaven must receive until the times of restoration of all things which God spoke by the mouth of his holy prophets' (Acts 3:19-21).

Two details matter. First, the 'all things' are qualified by 'which God spoke by the prophets'. Some grammarians read this as 'the restoration of all the things the prophets promised', limiting the scope to what was prophesied. Others say the prophets themselves promised a cosmic renewal, so the scope is still very wide. Second, the setting echoes the disciples' question about restoring the kingdom to Israel (Acts 1:6). Many commentators therefore read Acts 3:21 first of all as the fulfilment of Israel's hopes: the return of the Messiah, the renewal of God's people and the blessing of all nations through Abraham's seed (Acts 3:25-26).

The same sermon also warns that anyone who will not listen to the prophet like Moses 'shall be destroyed from among the people' (Acts 3:23). Traditional readers think this rules out a universalist reading here; universalist readers reply that warnings of judgment and a final restoration can both be true if judgment is not the last word.
19202:
Several of Paul's letters use 'all' language about the end. God's plan is 'to unite all things in Christ, things in heaven and things on earth' (Eph 1:10). Through Christ God was pleased 'to reconcile to himself all things, whether on earth or in heaven, making peace by the blood of his cross' (Col 1:20). At the end Christ hands the kingdom to the Father 'that God may be all in all' (1 Cor 15:24-28). God 'has consigned all to disobedience, that he may have mercy on all' (Rom 11:32). Every knee will bow and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord (Phil 2:10-11). Paul also writes, 'as in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive' (1 Cor 15:22), and 'one act of righteousness leads to justification and life for all men' (Rom 5:18).

These texts are the heart of the debate. They can be read as: (1) God restoring his creation and his people as a whole; (2) God pacifying all hostile powers, bringing everything under Christ's rule, whether willingly or not; or (3) God actually reconciling every person, so that every bended knee is a glad one.

Context matters for each. Romans 11:32 comes at the end of a discussion of Jews and Gentiles as groups. Philippians 2:10-11 quotes Isaiah 45:23, where the bowing includes those who were 'incensed' against God and are 'put to shame' (Isa 45:24). Colossians 1:20 is followed by a condition: 'if indeed you continue in the faith' (Col 1:23). Universalist readers answer that the same 'all' is used on both sides of Adam and Christ (1 Cor 15:22, Rom 5:18), and that 'confess' in scripture is usually the language of praise, not forced surrender.
19203: Reading 1: the restoration of Israel and the kingdom
19204:
On this reading, 'restoration' is about God keeping his promises to Israel. The prophets foresaw the return of the scattered tribes, a renewed covenant, a restored Jerusalem and the nations streaming to worship (Jer 31:31-34, Isa 2:2-4, Amos 9:11-12). Jesus chooses twelve apostles who will 'sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel' at 'the renewal' (Matt 19:28). Acts 15 quotes Amos about rebuilding David's fallen tent as Gentiles join God's people (Acts 15:16-17).

Different traditions fill this in differently. Dispensational and many Messianic Jewish readers expect a future national restoration of Israel in the land. Others (much Reformed and Catholic interpretation) see the restoration fulfilled in Christ and the church, Jew and Gentile together, with perhaps a future large-scale turning of Jewish people to Christ (Rom 11:25-27). Either way, the focus is on God's people and kingdom, not on each individual human.
19205: How Israel's restoration is fulfilled is itself a major debate (see the Israel and the Church debate). Scholars agree that Acts 1:6 and 3:21 are about Israel's hope; they disagree about whether that hope is fulfilled mainly in the church or still awaits a national fulfilment.
19207:
On this reading, the restoration of all things is the healing of the whole created order: the 'renewal of all things' (Matt 19:28), creation set free from decay (Rom 8:19-23), and the new heaven and new earth (Rev 21:1-5). 'All things' in Colossians 1:20 and Ephesians 1:10 includes 'things in heaven and on earth', the whole cosmos, not just people.

This was a major theme for Irenaeus, who spoke of creation being restored to its original state and made to serve the righteous. It is common today in Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant theology. It is compatible with believing in a final judgment in which some are lost, because what is restored is creation as such, purified of evil, not necessarily every individual within it. Revelation, for example, describes a renewed city with some still 'outside' (Rev 22:14-15).

Critics from the universalist side ask whether a creation can be truly 'restored' and God truly 'all in all' while some of his creatures remain forever in rebellion or torment. Defenders reply that God being all in all can include just judgment, and that evil is defeated even if not every evildoer is reconciled.
19208: Reading 3: universal reconciliation of all persons
19209:
On this reading, God will in the end bring every person into loving union with himself, through and after judgment. Punishment is real and may be long and severe, but it is remedial, like a refiner's fire (Mal 3:2-3, 1 Cor 3:13-15), not endless.

Clement of Alexandria described divine punishment as corrective. Origen (died about 253) taught that all rational beings, having fallen, would through long ages of education and purification return to God; whether he included the devil was disputed even in his lifetime. Gregory of Nyssa, a revered fourth-century bishop and defender of the Nicene Creed, taught that evil is finite and will be emptied out, so that in the end God will be 'all in all' with no one left outside (*On the Soul and the Resurrection*, *Catechetical Oration* 26). Isaac the Syrian, a seventh-century bishop and monk loved in Eastern spirituality, wrote that the 'scourge of love' in Gehenna serves God's purpose of mercy and expressed hope for the final good of all. Augustine noted that in his day many Christians, whom he called 'the merciful', hoped for an end to punishment, and he argued against them.

Modern defenders include Thomas Talbott (*The Inescapable Love of God*), Robin Parry (*The Evangelical Universalist*, first published under the pen name Gregory MacDonald) and David Bentley Hart (*That All Shall Be Saved*). Their main arguments are: the 'all' texts above; God's character as perfect love who 'desires all people to be saved' (1 Tim 2:4); the claim that a free creature fully seeing the truth could not forever reject the Good; and the moral difficulty of endless punishment for finite sins. Some Christians, such as Hans Urs von Balthasar, stop short of universalism and speak instead of a legitimate hope that all may be saved.
19210: Myth: 'Christian universalists deny hell and judgment.' Correction: most Christian universalists affirm that hell is real and that sin will be judged, sometimes severely and for long ages. What they deny is that it is endless or that it is God's final word for anyone.
19212:
Most of the church, East and West, has held that some will finally be lost. Their main objections to universal restoration are these.

Explicit texts of final judgment. Jesus contrasts 'eternal punishment' with 'eternal life' using the same adjective (Matt 25:46). He speaks of a sin that will not be forgiven 'in this age or in the age to come' (Matt 12:32), of the unquenchable fire (Mark 9:43-48), and of Judas, that it would have been better for him not to have been born (Mark 14:21). Paul speaks of 'eternal destruction' away from the Lord's presence (2 Thess 1:9). Revelation describes a lake of fire with no hint of exit (Rev 20:10, Rev 20:14-15).

Context of the 'all' texts. Critics argue that Paul's 'all' often means 'all kinds' (Jews and Gentiles) or 'all who are in Christ' (1 Cor 15:22-23 goes on, 'those who belong to Christ'), and that the cosmic reconciliation of Colossians 1:20 can mean the subduing of enemies, not their conversion (Col 2:15).

Freedom and love. If God's love respects human freedom, some may freely and finally refuse it; C. S. Lewis put it that the doors of hell are 'locked on the inside'. Urgency. Critics worry universalism weakens the call to repent and to mission (Heb 9:27, 2 Cor 6:2).

Universalists reply that *aiōnios* can mean 'of the age to come' rather than 'endless' (see 'Heaven and Hell Explained'); that 'not in this age or the age to come' speaks of these ages, not of all eternity; that true freedom is oriented to the good; and that the early universalists were fervent preachers of repentance.
19214:
In 543 the emperor Justinian issued an edict against Origen's teachings, with a list of anathemas (formal condemnations), approved by a local synod in Constantinople. One condemned the idea that the punishment of demons and wicked people is temporary and will end in a restoration. In 553 the Second Council of Constantinople, the fifth ecumenical council, met mainly to deal with a different controversy (the 'Three Chapters'). Its canon 11 lists Origen among heretics. A separate set of fifteen anathemas against Origenist teachings, beginning with the pre-existence of souls and 'the monstrous restoration that follows from it', is associated with the council.

Historians debate what this settled. Points in dispute include: whether the fifteen anathemas were formally approved by the ecumenical council or only by bishops gathered just before it opened; whether Origen's name in canon 11 was original; and whether the condemnations target universal salvation as such or a specific sixth-century Origenist system (pre-existent minds, a return to pure spirit, spherical resurrection bodies) linked with Evagrius. Notably, Gregory of Nyssa, who taught universal restoration without pre-existence, was never condemned and is venerated as a saint.

Scholars such as Ilaria Ramelli argue that the church never condemned universal hope as such. Scholars such as Brian Daley and Michael McClymond hold that, whatever the procedural details, the church received these condemnations as rejecting Origenist universalism, and that the later tradition overwhelmingly treated endless punishment as church teaching. Readers should treat the precise binding force of 553 as an open historical question.
19215: Myth: 'Origen was condemned for universalism at the Council of Nicaea.' Correction: Nicaea (325) dealt with Arius and did not address Origen. The formal condemnations came in 543 and 553, about three centuries after Origen's death, and what exactly they condemned is debated.

19271: What does the Bible actually say about heaven and hell, and what are the main Christian views?
19272: The Bible uses several different words that English Bibles often flatten into 'hell': Sheol and Hades (the realm of the dead), Gehenna (a place of final judgment named after a valley outside Jerusalem), Tartarus (a prison for rebel angels) and the lake of fire. Christians agree that God will judge evil and that the outcome is serious, but they hold three main views of what final judgment means: endless conscious punishment, final destruction of the wicked (conditional immortality), or a punishment that finally leads everyone to God (Christian universalism). On heaven, some stress going to be with God in heaven, while others stress that the final goal is resurrection on a renewed earth; many hold both, in two stages. Each view has serious biblical arguments, real weaknesses and thoughtful defenders.
19273: 'Hell' in English Bibles translates several different words with different meanings; reading them carefully prevents a lot of confusion.
19274: Sheol and Hades usually mean the realm of the dead, not the place of final punishment.
19275: Eternal conscious torment has been the majority view in church history; conditional immortality and universalism both have early roots and serious modern defenders.
19276: Much of the debate turns on a few words: 'eternal' (aiōnios), 'destroy', 'death', 'all'.
19277: Each view is regularly caricatured; the strongest versions are more careful than their critics often allow.
19278: On heaven, the biggest divide is about emphasis: going to God in heaven, or God coming to a renewed earth; most traditions affirm both in sequence.
19279: Sheol and Hades: the realm of the dead
19280:
In the Old Testament, the dead go down to Sheol. It is pictured as a dark, silent place under the earth where both good and bad people go (Gen 37:35, Eccl 9:10). The psalmists worry that in Sheol no one praises God (Ps 6:5, Ps 88:10-12), but they also hope God will not abandon them there (Ps 16:10, Ps 49:15). Older translations such as the King James Version sometimes render Sheol as 'hell', which misleads modern readers into thinking of a place of punishment.

The Greek Old Testament translated Sheol as Hades, and the New Testament uses Hades the same way: the realm of the dead. Jesus says the gates of Hades will not overcome his church (Matt 16:18); Peter says Jesus was not abandoned to Hades (Acts 2:27); the risen Christ holds 'the keys of Death and Hades' (Rev 1:18). In the parable of the rich man and Lazarus, Hades has a place of torment and a place of comfort (Luke 16:23). At the end, Death and Hades themselves are thrown into the lake of fire (Rev 20:13-14), which shows that Hades is temporary.

In short, Sheol and Hades mostly describe where the dead are now, not the final destiny.
19281: Myth: 'Every time the Bible says hell it means the place of eternal fire.' Correction: many older 'hell' passages translate Sheol or Hades, the realm of all the dead. Jacob expects to go to Sheol mourning his son (Gen 37:35); that is not a fear of damnation.
19282: Gehenna, Tartarus and the lake of fire
19283:
Gehenna is the word Jesus uses most for final judgment (Matt 5:22, Matt 10:28, Mark 9:43-48). It comes from the Valley of Hinnom on the south side of Jerusalem, where some kings of Judah had sacrificed children by fire (2 Kgs 23:10, Jer 7:31-32). Jeremiah prophesied it would become a 'valley of slaughter' full of corpses. By Jesus' time, Jewish writings used Gehenna as the name for the place of punishment after judgment. Jesus describes it with fire that is not quenched and the worm that does not die, quoting the last verse of Isaiah (Mark 9:48, Isa 66:24).

Tartarus appears once, as a verb: God 'cast them into Tartarus' about angels who sinned, holding them in chains of darkness until the judgment (2 Pet 2:4). In Greek myth Tartarus was the deepest prison of the underworld. Peter borrows the word for the holding place of fallen angels, not human beings.

The lake of fire appears only in Revelation. The beast and false prophet are thrown into it, then the devil, then Death and Hades, and then anyone not found in the book of life (Rev 19:20, Rev 20:10, Rev 20:14-15). Revelation calls it 'the second death' (Rev 20:14, Rev 21:8). How literally to take its fire, and what 'second death' implies, is part of the debate below.
19284: Myth: 'Gehenna was Jerusalem's burning rubbish dump, and Jesus just meant the town dump.' Correction: there is no ancient evidence for a perpetually burning dump in the Hinnom valley. The idea is usually traced to the medieval Jewish commentator David Kimhi (around 1200). Gehenna's power came from its history of child sacrifice and Jeremiah's prophecy of judgment, and by Jesus' day it was already a name for final punishment.
19286:
The Greek adjective *aiōnios* comes from *aiōn*, 'age'. It appears in 'eternal life' and also in 'eternal punishment', 'eternal fire' and 'eternal destruction' (Matt 25:46, Jude 1:7, 2 Thess 1:9). How it is understood shapes each view.

Traditional readers note that in Matthew 25:46 the same word describes life and punishment side by side, so if the life is endless the punishment must be too. Conditionalists usually agree that *aiōnios* means everlasting but argue it often describes the result, not an ongoing process: 'eternal destruction' is a destruction whose result lasts forever, just as 'eternal redemption' (Heb 9:12) is a redemption done once with permanent effects. Universalists, following scholars such as Ilaria Ramelli and David Konstan, argue that *aiōnios* in Jewish and Christian Greek often means 'belonging to the age to come' rather than strictly 'endless', so 'eternal punishment' could mean 'the punishment of the coming age', with its duration left open.

The word alone cannot settle the debate. Each side must also explain the wider context and other texts. Readers should notice which meaning a translation or teacher is assuming.
